text_used.text: English quotations of Cyprian, Pontius and the council are checked word for word against R. E. Wallis's translation in the Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1886), downloaded whole from CCEL (plain text, marked Public Domain) and split into one file per work. The court record (Acts of Cyprian) is quoted from E. C. E. Owen's translation (Oxford 1927; US public domain since 2023), checked against archive.org's OCR, with the Latin from Ruinart. 'exact' is the text as printed (footnote numbers removed); 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God.
text_used.note: Letter numbers: ANF (and New Advent) follow Migne's order, printing To Donatus as Epistle 1. The modern (Hartel, Oxford) numbers differ; ANF gives the Oxford number in a footnote to each letter, recorded below as 'Oxford N'. Chapter pages on CCEL: Pontius anf05.iv.iii, Epistle N anf05.iv.iv.<roman N>, Treatise N anf05.iv.v.<roman N>, the council anf05.iv.vi.i. All CCEL and New Advent pages cited were fetched on 2026-09-24 (HTTP 200) and checked to contain the quoted line. New Advent's copy of Wallis matches the CCEL text for every line checked here.

who_draft.text: Cyprian was a rich teacher of public speaking in Carthage who became a Christian about 246 and its bishop two years later. He led his church through persecution, plague and quarrels, often by letter from hiding. He argued hard with the bishop of Rome. In 258 he was beheaded, the first bishop of Carthage to die a martyr.
who_draft.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 67; Catholic Encyclopedia (1908); Pontius, Life 19
who_draft.note: 56 words. 'Teacher of public speaking' = Jerome's 'teacher of rhetoric'.

why_dates_differ.text: He died on 14 September. Jerome says he died on the same day of the year as Pope Cornelius, though not in the same year, and the West keeps the two together on the 16th. The 14th is also Holy Cross Day, and the Church of England (15th) and the Episcopal Church (13th) set him beside it. The old Prayer Book's 26 September is the Western day of the other, legendary Cyprian of Antioch and Justina, a sign of the old confusion between the two men.
why_dates_differ.source: Acts of Cyprian 3 (14 September); Jerome, Lives 67; Roman Martyrology (1916); CofE and Episcopal calendars (14 September Holy Cross Day); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Sts. Cyprian and Justina' (26 September)

life_moments.title: A new man
life_moments.text: An older priest named Caecilius brought him to faith. Cyprian had thought a man could never shed habits so deep. After baptism, he wrote, what had seemed impossible became possible. He sold whole estates for the poor. When Caecilius died, he left Cyprian his wife and children to look after.

life_moments.title: Leading by letter
life_moments.text: When the emperor Decius ordered everyone to sacrifice to the gods, crowds shouted for Cyprian to be thrown to the lions. He went into hiding and ran his church by letter. The clergy at Rome wrote that he had acted 'quite rightly', then pointedly quoted the hireling who runs from the wolf. He sent them thirteen of his letters to show what he had done.

life_moments.title: Second chances
life_moments.text: Thousands had denied the faith under Decius, and many wanted back in. Cyprian chose a middle way: real penance, then return. He admitted he had been harsher at first. At Rome, Novatian refused the fallen any return and set himself up as a rival bishop. Cyprian answered with his book On the Unity of the Church.

life_moments.title: The quarrel with Rome
life_moments.text: Cyprian held that anyone baptised by heretics must be baptised again. Pope Stephen said no: only hands should be laid on them. Stephen was, in Eusebius's words, 'very indignant'. Stephen refused even to receive Cyprian's messengers. Cyprian's council of 87 bishops stood with him. Neither side gave way. After this, says the Catholic Encyclopedia, 'we know no more of the controversy.'

life_moments.title: Exile, and a dream
life_moments.text: Under the emperor Valerian he was tried and sent into exile at Curubis, on the coast. He told the proconsul, 'I am a Christian and a bishop.' On his first night there he dreamed of a young man who showed him, with a flat hand like a blade, the sentence to come. He asked for one day's delay and was given it. Pontius says the day meant a year: he died exactly a year later.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: St Cyprian was a magician converted by the virgin Justina, and 'the Prayer of St Cyprian' against witchcraft is his.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: That is Cyprian of Antioch, a legendary figure. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Gregory of Nazianzus and Prudentius already 'confounded our Cyprian with St. Cyprian of Carthage, a mistake often repeated', and that 'no Bishop of Antioch bore the name of Cyprian'. misquoted_or_legend.claim: Cyprian taught that the Church is founded on the chair of Peter and the pope's primacy.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Chapter 4 of On the Unity of the Church survives in two forms. One has 'the primacy is given to Peter' and 'He who deserts the chair of Peter'. The Protestant editors of the Ante-Nicene Fathers called these words 'beyond all question spurious'. The Catholic Encyclopedia says it is 'now generally admitted' that Cyprian himself made the change, and that by 'one chair' he always meant the bishop's chair. Both sides agree he taught that all the apostles had equal power.

hard_topics.text: The Western Church later followed Stephen. Augustine says Cyprian held 'an opinion at variance with the true view' but stayed in unity and was cleansed by martyrdom. Jerome claims the African bishops later went back to the old custom. The ANF American editor (Coxe, an Episcopal bishop) wrote that 'on the Roman theory' Cyprian 'died in schism', yet is a canonized saint.

how_he_died.text: Recalled from exile in 258, he waited in his gardens at Carthage. Friends begged him to flee; he refused, but hid once so he would not be tried at Utica. On 13 September he was arrested and kept overnight, with his people watching outside. On 14 September the proconsul Galerius Maximus asked him to perform the Roman rites. He said, 'I refuse.' Told to consider his own interest, he answered, 'Do as you are bid. In so clear a case there is no need for consideration.' The proconsul, 'hardly and reluctantly', sentenced him to die by the sword. Cyprian said, 'Thanks be to God!' The crowd cried, 'Let us also be beheaded with him.' Led out, he knelt and prayed, took off his cloak, and told his friends to give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces. He tied his own blindfold; a priest and a subdeacon fastened the ends. Pontius says the executioner's hand shook so that he could hardly hold the sword, until strength was given to the centurion 'from above'.

later.text: The Acts add that his body was laid out for the pagans to see, then carried at night with candles and torches to the cemetery of Macrobius Candidianus. is_he_a_saint.text: Yes. Catholics keep him with Pope Cornelius on 16 September, and his name is among the martyrs of the Roman Canon, the Mass's traditional Eucharistic Prayer. The Orthodox honour him as a hieromartyr (31 August in the OCA and the Russian Church), though Greek calendars merge him with Cyprian of Antioch. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep him, and Lutherans commemorate him.

He was honoured from the start: the Acts call him 'the most blessed martyr', and Augustine preached on his feast. Possible quote for the page: Augustine's 'pruning-hook of martyrdom' line (others_on_him).

prayer_he_wrote.text: No prayer composed by him survives as a separate prayer. His treatise On the Lord's Prayer explains the Our Father line by line. The 'Prayer of St Cyprian' sold today belongs to the legend of Cyprian of Antioch. If the page wants his words in a prayerful voice, the close of On Mortality is his: 'May God behold this our eager desire; may the Lord Christ look upon this purpose of our mind and faith, He who will give the larger rewards of His glory to those whose desires in respect of Himself were greater!'

hub_card.text: Hints confirmed: a Latin Church Father (fathers) and a martyr (martyrs); died 258 (pre300); a Latin bishop in Africa (west). He is honoured East and West, but he wrote in Latin and belongs to the Latin West, as Martin does.
hub_card.note: Not 'teachers' unless that group means Latin writers generally: Jerome and Lactantius rank him the first great Latin Christian writer after Tertullian (CE 1908: 'the first great Latin writer among the Christians').

site_data_flags.text: people.cyprian.hook: 'Then he had his friends give the executioner twenty-five gold coins.' Right order (sentence, 'Thanks be to God', then the coins when the executioner came). Owen: 'twenty-five golden pieces'. The Oxford editor suspected the gift was a copyist's addition; Ruinart kept it because every manuscript he saw had it.

people.cyprian.cells.tell.work is 'Testimonies against the Jews' (ANF's title). The book is addressed to Quirinus and Book 3 (where heading 77 is) is ethics, not about Jews. Consider 'Testimonies, to Quirinus'.
people.cyprian.cells.calling: the line is Cyprian's own heading over Bible texts, not a sentence of argument. Fine to show, but the page could say so.

pairs.tertullian: 'Jerome says Cyprian read Tertullian every day and called him the master.' Jerome had it second-hand from Cyprian's old secretary, Paul of Concordia. Consider 'Jerome heard that...'.
Research status_note gave 'the Orthodox Church (31 August)'. True for the OCA and the Russian Church only; Greek calendars merge him with Cyprian of Antioch on 2 October.
Research also said 'Julius' for the two helpers at his blindfold (CE); Owen's Acts have 'the priest Julianus and Julianus the sub-deacon'.

script_check.text: Every 'exact' quotation was searched for in its local fetched file after normalising whitespace, curly quotes, the æ ligature, footnote numbers and spaces before punctuation (case-insensitive).

items: Died/death.big: 'just outside Carthage' -> 'near Carthage'. The 1916 Roman Martyrology (14 September) puts the martyrdom 'near the seashore, six miles from the city'; the Acts say only 'the land of Sextus'.

Buried/later: 'the same night', 'that night' -> 'by night'; 'outside Carthage' dropped. Acts 5.6 (Owen): 'Thence it was removed by night, and, accompanied by tapers and torches ... to the burial-ground of Macrobius Candidianus the procurator, which lies on the Mappalian way near the fishponds.'
Also called: 'Thascius was his own name' replaced. Acts 3.3: 'Are you Thascius Cyprianus?'; ANF intro: 'At his baptism he assumed the name of his friend Caecilius'.
Florentius Puppianus: not 'a layman' in the source. Letter 68.4: 'the persecution, when it came, lifted you to the highest sublimity of martyrdom' (a confessor).
Jerome, Letter 58: 'about 394' -> 'about 395', as the cited NPNF/New Advent heading says ('Written about the year 395 A.D.').

Circle, Cornelius: 'They died on the same day of the year' stated as fact -> attributed to Jerome (Illustrious Men 67). CE puts Cornelius's death at Centumcellae about June 253; the ANF intro says 14 September 252.

Roman Canon: 'Of the twelve martyrs it names, he is the only one who was not a saint of Rome itself' was wrong: the Canon also names martyrs in the Nobis quoque list (Ignatius, Perpetua, Felicity, Agatha, Lucy...). CE (Canon of the Mass) speaks of the twelve martyrs of the first (Communicantes) list: 'All these saints, except St. Cyprian, are local Roman saints'. Now attributed to CE.

Greek calendars: 'give him no day of his own' was too broad. Koinonia Orthodoxias prints his own life from Makarios of Simonopetra, New Synaxaristis, vol. 1 September (Ormylia 2001), p. 179. Now 'Popular Greek calendars' plus that exception, and the source is listed.

Extra ecclesiam nulla salus: 'came later' (unsourced date) replaced. His Latin as quoted by Papadopoulos's Patrology (sostis.gr): 'salus extra ecclesiam non est' (Ep. 73.21 = ANF 72); NPNF 2.6 calls the neat form 'the maxim of Cyprian'.

Primacy myth: 'The Protestant editors' -> 'The notes to the English translation'. Note 3110 is unbracketed (the Edinburgh translator's, not Coxe's) and the translator's church is not in a fetched source.
On the Lapsed 25: 'At once she was sick' -> 'Then she sobbed and was sick' ('Then there followed a sobbing and vomiting'). Chapter 26: 'in a box at home' -> 'in a box' (the text says only 'her box').

Letter 60: 'an actor who taught the stage' -> 'an actor who no longer performed but still taught acting' (argument: he 'Himself Does Not Practice the Histrionic Art, So Long as He Teaches It to Others').
To Donatus: 'Cyprian had thought no one could shed habits as deep as his' -> 'had not believed he could ever shed' (ch. 4: 'from which I did not believe that I could by possibility be delivered').
Second chances: 'most wanted to come back' -> 'many' (no source gives a share).
Death: 'ordered him to perform the Roman rites' -> 'told him the emperors commanded him to perform the rite' (Acts 3.5, Owen).
Lactantius: 'a learned pagan' -> 'a clever critic' ('a certain man who was skilful indeed').
Visions: title 'Doubted by his own translators' -> 'Doubted by his English editor' (one editor doubted; the American editor defended).
Coxe as an Episcopal bishop: confirmed (second Episcopal bishop of Western New York, Wikipedia 'Arthur Cleveland Coxe').
Five inline quotations in death and saint paragraphs had no evidence entries under the updated verifier: added to cyprian-of-carthage.quotes.json (Owen Acts 3.6, 4.1, 5.1, 6; Pontius 18).
